title: Tokenization could unleash tens of billions of dollars in trapped capital, Nasdaq CEO says
content: Tokenization could free up tens of billions of dollars in capital tied up in assets used as collateral across the global financial system, Nasdaq CEO Adena Friedman said. Tokenizing assets such as Treasurys, equities and money market funds, along with the flow of money, could make collateral more liquid, Friedman told CNBC's Joanna Ossinger , managing editor and head of APAC Digital News, at the TOKEN2049 conference in Singapore. "If you tokenize all those instruments along with the flow of money, then the collateral becomes very fluid," Friedman said. Tokenization involves representing financial assets, such as stocks and bonds, as digital tokens that can be transferred using blockchain technology. Friedman said institutional interest in tokenization has grown over the past year, pointing in part to the passage of the Genius Act in the U.S., which established a regulatory framework for stablecoins. "If we can tokenize money, then we can tokenize the flow of capital," she said. That growing institutional interest is converging with demand from retail investors, who have long sought the ability to trade around the clock, according to Friedman. The retail ecosystem "has been about 10 years ahead," she said. Moving to a fully 24/7 market would be a major undertaking for the financial industry, Friedman said. "The easiest part is the exchange infrastructure," she said. Friedman said that financial institutions have traditionally had periods when markets are closed to update systems and manage risk. But operating around the clock would require those processes, including risk and collateral management, to take place continuously. "Everything has to be real time all the time," she said. Artificial intelligence could help financial institutions manage that transition. Nasdaq has launched a series of digital agents within its risk management platform that initially provide recommendations, Friedman said. Over time, banks could use those agents to take more direct action, she added. "AI is critical for 24/7," Friedman said. Companies outside the U.S. are showing interest in tokenization and access to American capital markets, Arjun Sethi, co-CEO of cryptocurrency exchange Kraken, told CNBC. Sethi pointed to a company generating roughly $25 million in revenue that was exploring ways to access capital markets, as well as larger international companies interested in tokenization and U.S. public listings. He said tokenization could help expand access to capital markets for companies around the world. However, round-the-clock trading may not be suitable for everything, according to Friedman. "Not every asset is liquid enough to support a 24/7 environment," she said. Still, greater connectivity across the global financial system could also open up access to asset classes that were previously out of reach for some investors, Friedman said.
ranking_reason: The potential for tokenization to free up tens of billions of dollars in trapped capital could have significant economic implications.

analysis.reason: The potential for tokenization to free up tens of billions of dollars in trapped capital could have significant economic implications.

title: 5 Things to Know
content: This is CNBC's Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox. Happy Thursday. Catch David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz , co-CEOs of the newly formed Skydance , on CNBC's "Squawk Box" this morning. Watch live on CNBC or CNBC+. Stock futures are lower before the bell. The three major indexes are coming off a losing day. Here are five key things investors need to know to start the trading day: Federal Reserve officials see another rate hike before the end of the year, according to minutes from their September meeting released yesterday. However, the document didn't give any clear hints as to when exactly policymakers thought that hike could come. Here's what else we're following: PepsiCo beat Wall Street's third-quarter expectations on both lines this morning, reporting a 5.6% jump in net sales as international markets continued to drive the beverage giant's growth. As CNBC's Amelia Lucas writes, 41% of Pepsi's net revenue so far this year is thanks to its international business. Its North America beverage division, on the other hand, continues to shrink as Pepsi pursues a domestic turnaround focused on ingredient innovation and advertising. Those home-court struggles are weighing on profits, leading Pepsi to slash its full-year earnings forecast with one quarter to go. PepsiCo CEO Ramon Laguarta will join CNBC at 10 a.m. ET for an exclusive interview. Click here to watch live. Crude oil prices are up more than 4% this morning after Trump said he no longer wants a deal with Iran . "I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop," the president said at a Wednesday night campaign rally in Texas. Trump's comments come after NBC News reported that he and his team have discussed potentially resuming military operations soon. Brent crude futures and U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures are both higher this morning on fears that hostilities in the Middle East may escalate once again. In an effort to ease the pain of record-high diesel prices, Trump signed an executive order earlier this week allowing truckers to use off-road diesel on highways without paying federal excise taxes. But analysts said that the order may only end up deferring those payments rather than removing them entirely. Microsoft's new laptop will come with an Nvidia chip and $2,599 price tag, the companies announced yesterday. Consumers can preorder the Surface Laptop Ultra now, and it will begin shipping next week. As CNBC's Jordan Novet writes, Microsoft has been trying to pack more artificial intelligence capabilities into its consumer devices. Microsoft also said yesterday that Meta would roll out a version of its Muse AI agent for Windows. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang are both among the slate of tech execs expected to be honored by Trump with medals today, CNBC confirmed. Tesla 's Elon Musk and Dell 's Michael Dell are also on the list for the event titled Science: A New Golden Age Summit. Megadonors are broadly backing Republicans this midterm election cycle, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Out of the 20 largest donors and donor groups, 14 are either exclusively or almost entirely backing GOP candidates or aligned groups. Democratic donors, meanwhile, have increasingly skipped over the Democratic National Committee, with some choosing to instead funnel money directly to candidates. Fundraisers told CNBC's Luke Fountain that Democratic donors have "trauma" from the last election cycle, as well as concerns about the DNC's leadership and the growing influence of the party's democratic socialist bloc. Between Labor Day and Sept. 25, conservative super PACs outspent Democratic counterparts by an almost 2-to-1 ratio, the FEC records show. The GOP is working — and spending — hard in hopes of keeping control of Washington, as once-safe districts are now seen as toss-ups. Buckle up: Wall Street is expecting another gangbusters earnings season. title: Russia's internet giant Yandex halts operations at major data center after drone attack
content: Russian internet giant Yandex suspended operations at one of its key data centers on Thursday after a drone strike as Ukraine continues to target the country's infrastructure. The attack caused a fire at the company's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan, in western Russia, and affected part of its infrastructure, Yandex said in a statement to CNBC. The data center has stopped operating entirely, and some Yandex services may be unavailable to users, it added. "There are no casualties, and emergency services are on site dealing with the aftermath," Yandex said. Moscow-headquartered Yandex, known as the Google of Russia, provides the country's most widely used search engine. It also developed the region's leading generative AI model, YandexGPT. Although Ukraine has not claimed responsibility for the Yandex attack, it has been stepping up its attacks on Russian infrastructure, including energy, over recent months, such as targeting Russian oil refineries , which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said are used to "finance the war and the killing of Ukrainians." Ukraine also increased attacks on Russian retail giant Wildberries , a critical part of the consumer infrastructure. Last week, Zelenskyy said the country will double down on its attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes from Moscow designed to force people to leave Kyiv and other cities. Emergency power cuts were enforced in Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, on Thursday due to ongoing Russian air strikes on the country's power grid. Last week, Russia hit key facilities in Kyiv and other major cities across the country, as it looks to destabilize Ukraine's energy foundation ahead of the winter season, threatening heating and other essential services for civilians. In response, Ukraine has been attacking Russia's fuel and energy facilities, with Zelenskyy warning Russian President Vladimir Putin at the United Nations General Assembly in September that Kyiv would make winter painful for Russia if the two sides were unable to come to an energy truce. "Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too," Zelenskyy said on Sept. 23.
